blocks.text:
There is a version of "design a video platform" that is really "design Netflix": a curated catalog, professionally encoded masters, a controlled ingestion pipeline. This is not that problem. This is the harder, messier version, where anyone with a phone and a spotty connection can upload anything at any moment, uploads can be gigabytes in size and can fail halfway through, and the system somehow needs to turn that chaos into a platform where a video someone just finished uploading from their bedroom can be watched by millions of people within minutes, with an accurate-enough view count and a comment thread underneath it.

That distinction, open, unmoderated, unpredictable user-generated uploads rather than a curated pipeline, is the thread that runs through this entire design. We are going to build a platform where creators upload video, the system processes it into multiple streamable qualities, viewers watch and interact with it, and the whole thing counts views, threads comments, and helps people find what to watch next.

blocks.content: ["Uploads use a chunked, resumable protocol, since large files over unreliable mobile connections are the common case, not the exception.","A \"view\" counts only after a viewer has watched at least a threshold duration (for example 30 seconds), to filter out accidental clicks and bot traffic from inflating counts.","Content moderation and copyright detection are acknowledged as necessary in a real system but treated as a separate, external pipeline for this design, not built out in depth.","Recommendations are computed in a periodic offline batch job, refreshed regularly, not calculated live on every single request.","Comments support one level of threaded replies for this design, not unlimited nesting."]
items: Uploads use a chunked, resumable protocol, since large files over unreliable mobile connections are the common case, not the exception.
A "view" counts only after a viewer has watched at least a threshold duration (for example 30 seconds), to filter out accidental clicks and bot traffic from inflating counts.
Content moderation and copyright detection are acknowledged as necessary in a real system but treated as a separate, external pipeline for this design, not built out in depth.
Recommendations are computed in a periodic offline batch job, refreshed regularly, not calculated live on every single request.
Comments support one level of threaded replies for this design, not unlimited nesting.

blocks.text: Suppose the platform sees 500 hours of video uploaded every minute platform-wide, a genuinely enormous, continuous stream of raw content, alongside 5 billion video views a day. That view volume works out to 5,000,000,000 divided by 86,400, or roughly 58,000 views per second on average, and a single video going unexpectedly viral can spike far beyond that average all on its own, easily into the tens of thousands of view events per second just for that one piece of content.

blocks.text: If each minute of uploaded video, once transcoded into multiple renditions (say six quality levels combined), averages roughly 500MB of total stored bytes, then 500 hours per minute, which is 30,000 minutes of raw footage every minute, times 500MB, is a genuinely staggering 15TB of new storage every single minute. Even accounting for the fact that raw uploads are compressed and only the most-watched renditions need to stay on hot storage, this number is why tiered, cost-aware storage (section 25) is not optional at this scale, it is load bearing.

blocks.text: The upload path and the playback path are almost entirely separate systems joined by shared video metadata. A creator uploads chunk by chunk to an upload service, which assembles and validates the file before handing it to an asynchronous transcoding pipeline; only once that pipeline finishes does a video become watchable. Playback, by contrast, almost never touches the upload path at all, it reads a manifest of available renditions and streams segments through a CDN.

blocks.title: Why chunk uploads are idempotent by chunk number
blocks.text: A mobile connection dropping mid-upload is not a rare edge case here, it is an expected, routine occurrence. If re-uploading a chunk that actually succeeded the first time (but whose acknowledgement was lost) created a duplicate or corrupted the assembled file, resumable upload would not actually be reliable. Keying each chunk upload by its chunk number, and having the server simply accept an already-received chunk as a no-op success, makes retries completely safe.

A worked example sequence diagram: Alice's upload drops mid transfer and resumes from the last confirmed chunk, gets transcoded, and Bob watches it later with his view counted only after crossing the watch threshold

blocks.text: Alice is uploading a fifteen-minute video from her phone on a train, and partway through, the connection drops entirely. Because the upload was chunked, she does not need to start over: her app queries the upload status endpoint, learns exactly which chunks already made it through, and resumes from the next one once she has signal again. Once every chunk is confirmed, the upload service assembles the complete file and enqueues a transcoding job. A few minutes later, transcoding finishes and the video flips to a ready status. Bob finds it later that day and starts watching; the player reports a view event once he has watched past the counting threshold, not the instant he taps play, so a viewer who clicks and immediately clicks away does not inflate the count.

The actual video segments themselves are effectively cached at the CDN edge layer, which is really the dominant caching strategy in this entire system, discussed in more depth as part of the architecture.

blocks.text: The transcoding pipeline is the clearest async workload in the system: uploads arrive in unpredictable bursts (a popular creator publishing at a scheduled time, a sudden trend causing many people to upload related content at once) and the queue absorbs that burst, letting a fixed or auto-scaling pool of workers process jobs at a sustainable, controlled rate rather than the upload path itself being coupled to processing capacity.

blocks.text: Upload, playback, and comment services are all stateless and load balance with straightforward round robin, with the one caveat that a long-running chunked upload session should ideally continue routing to a consistent backend for the duration of that session to avoid unnecessary cross-instance state lookups, though the design does not strictly require it since upload state itself lives in shared storage, not instance memory.

blocks.text: Transcoding workers scale off queue depth, the same pattern used elsewhere for bursty async pipelines. Playback and API services scale off request rate in the conventional way, with playback typically needing far more capacity than upload given the roughly 99 to 1 view-to-upload ratio established in the capacity estimates.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing the choice of availability plus eventual consistency, justified by the fact that a view count or comment ordering being a few seconds stale is harmless

blocks.text: View counts, like counts, and even comment visibility ordering all tolerate a small amount of staleness without any real user-facing harm, so this system leans firmly toward availability. The one place needing real care is upload chunk tracking itself: losing track of which chunks were actually received would break resumability entirely, so that specific piece of state is written with stronger durability guarantees than the rest of the system.

blocks.text: Transcoding jobs are retried automatically on worker failure, since a job is naturally idempotent (re-running it just regenerates the same renditions). Playback, being read-heavy and served largely through the CDN, is resilient to origin-side issues for any content already cached at the edge, which given typical view patterns is the vast majority of actual playback traffic.

blocks.text: Beyond standard authentication and rate limiting on upload and comment endpoints, an open upload platform genuinely needs automated content moderation and copyright detection as a security-adjacent concern unique to user-generated content at this scale, screening uploads for known-infringing or clearly abusive material before or shortly after they become publicly playable. This is treated as an external pipeline for this design per the assumptions, but it is worth naming explicitly since it is the single biggest practical risk of an open upload model.

blocks.text: The signals that matter most are transcoding queue depth and job failure rate (a backlog here directly delays creators from being watchable), playback start latency and rebuffer rate per CDN region, and view-count aggregator flush lag. A sustained spike in transcoding failures for a particular input format is often the earliest sign of an upstream codec or format-handling bug worth investigating immediately.

blocks.alt: A map of two bottlenecks: the transcoding queue backing up during upload bursts, fixed by auto scaling the worker pool off queue depth, and a video going viral overnight, fixed by CDN absorption of playback traffic

blocks.text: A burst of simultaneous uploads, say from a viral trend prompting thousands of creators to post related content at once, is the clearest write-side bottleneck, addressed by auto-scaling transcoding capacity against queue depth. On the read side, a single video going unexpectedly viral overnight is handled the way it always is in a CDN-fronted architecture: the edge cache absorbs nearly all of that traffic before it ever threatens origin storage.

blocks.text: Defining a "view" as requiring a minimum watch duration, rather than counting every playback start, is a deliberate trade: it produces a more meaningful, harder-to-game number at the cost of slightly more complex client-side and event-aggregation logic than a naive click counter would need. Batch-computed recommendations, rather than live personalized ranking on every request, trade some freshness (a just-watched video will not immediately reshape recommendations) for dramatically lower serving-time cost and complexity, which is the right call for the vast majority of a general-purpose recommendation feed.

items: An upload session is abandoned partway through and never resumed, requiring a cleanup job to eventually reclaim the partial chunks sitting in storage.
A malformed or corrupted video file fails transcoding entirely, needing a clear failed state rather than an indefinitely stuck processing status.
A comment reply is posted to a comment that was deleted moments earlier, requiring a defined behavior (orphaned reply still shown, or reply rejected) rather than an undefined error.
A video receives an enormous, sudden burst of view events far exceeding normal traffic, which the view aggregator needs to absorb without falling critically behind.

blocks.text: This design covers a resumable, checksum-verified chunked upload protocol built for unreliable connections, an asynchronous transcoding pipeline that scales against unpredictable upload bursts, a threshold-based view counting model resistant to accidental and low-effort gaming, tiered storage to control the cost of an ever-growing catalog, and a batch-refreshed search and recommendation layer kept deliberately separate from the low-latency playback path.
